title: Autonomous weapons: should the world negotiate a treaty?
summary: The General Assembly debates whether to start treaty negotiations on lethal autonomous weapons systems, what a treaty should ban, whether there should be a deadline, and which forum should host the talks.

committee.name: General Assembly: lethal autonomous weapons systems (practice)
committee.notes: A practice draft written for class; not an adopted UN text. Positions are estimates from the linked UN voting records.

topic.name: Lethal autonomous weapons systems
topic.notes: Real topic. The draft resolution is a practice text written for class. Country positions are estimates drawn from recorded votes on General Assembly resolutions 78/241 (2023) and 79/62 (2024) and are not statements of fact; countries not listed have no recorded estimate.

tags.binding_treaty: Starts negotiations on a legally binding international instrument
tags.human_control: Requires meaningful human control over decisions to use force
tags.prohibitions: Bans autonomous weapons that cannot be used with meaningful human control
tags.target_people: Bans autonomous weapons designed to select and attack human beings
tags.deadline: Sets a fixed deadline for the negotiations to finish
tags.un_forum: Holds the talks in an open General Assembly process
tags.ccw_forum: Keeps expert work in the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (Geneva)
tags.moratorium: Asks States to hold back new systems until a treaty is in force

resolution.title: Lethal autonomous weapons systems: a practice draft

preambular.text: Recalling the purposes and principles of the Charter of the United Nations, including the maintenance of international peace and security,
Reaffirming that international law, including international humanitarian law, applies to all weapons, including autonomous weapons systems,
Recalling General Assembly resolutions 78/241 and 79/62 on lethal autonomous weapons systems,
Noting the work of the Group of Governmental Experts under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons,
Taking note of the report of the Secretary-General on lethal autonomous weapons systems,

operative.text: Decides to begin negotiations on a legally binding instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems;
Affirms that humans must keep meaningful control over any decision to use force, including a decision to take human life;
Decides that the instrument shall prohibit autonomous weapons systems that cannot be used with meaningful human control, and shall regulate all other such systems;
Further decides that the instrument shall prohibit autonomous weapons systems designed to select and attack human beings;
Sets a deadline of two years from the adoption of this resolution for the negotiations to conclude;
Decides that the negotiations shall take place in an open process under the General Assembly, in which every Member State has an equal voice;
Requests the Group of Governmental Experts under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva to continue its work and to share its findings with the negotiations;
Urges States not to deploy new autonomous weapons systems that select and attack targets without meaningful human control until the instrument enters into force.

cards.text: Requests the Secretary-General to hold consultations with Member States on whether and how a legally binding instrument could be negotiated;
Decides that the negotiations shall aim to finish within four years, with a progress review after two years;
Encourages the negotiating process to finish its work within a reasonable time, without a fixed date;
Decides that the negotiations shall take place in the General Assembly, drawing on the findings of the Group of Governmental Experts and inviting its chair to report to each session;
Encourages States to adopt national rules on meaningful human control and to share them voluntarily while negotiations continue;
Calls upon States to review every new weapon for compliance with international humanitarian law before use, and to publish how they carry out the review;
Urges States to refrain from developing autonomous weapons systems designed to select and attack human beings;
Decides that the instrument shall use a definition of meaningful human control prepared with technical experts and humanitarian organisations;

events.title: A regional group meets before the vote
events.body: Delegates from one region meet to compare positions. Whoever has been working with them most finds a warmer welcome when they speak.
events.teaches: Regional groups often settle on a common line before the formal meeting, so time spent with them pays off.

events.title: New instructions from a capital on the forum
events.body: A capital sends fresh instructions about where the talks should be held. Delegations that want an open General Assembly process speak up more firmly.
events.teaches: Delegates act on instructions from their capitals, and those can change during a negotiation.

events.title: A technical expert briefs delegates on human control
events.body: A technical expert explains how different systems keep a person in the decision. Delegates ask what counts as meaningful control, and the question dominates the room.
events.teaches: Experts help delegates understand what a text would mean in practice, though they do not decide the vote.

events.title: An NGO side event on systems that target people
events.body: A non-governmental organisation holds a side event on weapons that select people as targets. Delegates return to the negotiation with the question on their minds.
events.teaches: Side events let delegations hear arguments away from formal meetings, which can shift where attention lands.

events.title: A co-sponsor hesitates over the deadline
events.body: A co-sponsor says it cannot support a fixed deadline without more time to consult its capital. You must spend more effort to keep your group together.
events.teaches: Co-sponsors can waver late, so holding a group together is a continuing job.

events.title: A revised draft circulates in the room
events.body: The facilitators hand round a revised draft with small changes in many clauses. Delegations stop to read it before they will talk about anything else.
events.teaches: Revised drafts reset the conversation, because each delegation must check every change against its instructions.

author: Claude Sonnet (delegated), 4 Nov 2026; to be checked by B. Gough
